title: Prediction of incident inflammatory bowel disease from routine electronic health records: development and external validation of a longitudinal machine learning model
authors: Onal, G.; Ayati, A.; Chen, M.-Y.; Mukherjee, A.; Rudrapatna, V. A.
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMSInflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin, and diagnostic delay is associated with complications. We tested whether longitudinal machine learning using electronic health record (EHR) data can identify incident IBD before diagnosis, and quantified lead time and deployment burden. METHODSWe studied adults with an IBD-compatible symptom, sign, or finding at UCSF (2012-2024). Incident cases were confirmed by structured filtering and validated large language model note review. We trained a state space model (Mamba) and comparators on pre-diagnostic EHR data, excluding diagnostic-workup features, and assessed discrimination at 6- and 12-month landmarks. We externally tested Mamba without recalibration at ZSFG, a safety-net hospital serving a demographically and socioeconomically distinct population, and simulated diagnosis-code-only deployment at UCSF. RESULTSSix months after presentation, among patients still undiagnosed (67% of UCSF test cases), Mamba achieved an AUROC of 0.969 (95% CI, 0.928-0.999) at UCSF and 0.965 (0.952-0.976) at ZSFG. Median lead time was 20 months at UCSF and 15 months at ZSFG. Among future cases with an initially normal colonoscopy (N=32) or a histological finding of acute inflammation without chronicity (N=63), the model flagged 84% and 89% of these patients, respectively, before those procedures, indicating the potential for pre-diagnostic detection. Among 358,886 symptomatic patients not used for training (60 incident cases), the diagnosis-code-only model achieved an AUROC of 0.926; reviewing 20 alerts/month identified 34 cases (PPV, 1.09%; 64-fold above baseline). CONCLUSIONSLongitudinal machine learning can identify increased IBD risk months to years before diagnosis and may define a population for prospective studies of early IBD biology. Prospective evaluation should determine whether earlier identification reduces diagnostic delay. What You Need to KnowO_ST_ABSBackground and ContextC_ST_ABSIBD is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin. Whether routinely collected electronic health record data can identify future IBD before diagnosis, and at what alert burden, is unknown. New FindingsA longitudinal model identified future IBD six months after first symptomatic presentation with an AUROC of 0.97 and a median lead time of 20 months, with similar external discrimination. LimitationsThis was a retrospective study; external case labels were inferred rather than adjudicated, and colonoscopy analyses were exploratory. Whether earlier flagging shortens time to diagnosis requires prospective evaluation. Clinical Research RelevanceRoutinely collected structured EHR data could support targeted gastroenterology review of recurrently symptomatic patients. Because incident IBD is rare among symptomatic patients, a service reviewing 20 flagged charts per month would identify roughly one future case every five months. Deployment should therefore begin in silent mode, with locally calibrated thresholds and prospective measurement of alert burden. Basic Research RelevanceThe model flagged most future cases before a pre-diagnostic colonoscopy read as normal, or before biopsies showing only acute inflammation. Patients flagged despite normal-appearing mucosa may represent a preclinical population in which the earliest immunologic, serologic, and microbial events of IBD could be studied prospectively, including through model-guided mucosal sampling. Lay SummaryAn AI system reviewing medical records data is able to identify people who would later be diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease, often more than a year before doctors made the diagnosis.

infographic.key_insight: A longitudinal machine learning model using routine EHR data could flag people at high risk for incident inflammatory bowel disease months to years before diagnosis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If prospectively validated, this approach could help clinicians find patients with undiagnosed IBD earlier and potentially shorten diagnostic delay.
method: Trained a Mamba state-space model on pre-diagnostic EHR data from adults with IBD-compatible symptoms/signs/finding.
Excluded diagnostic-workup features to focus on pre-workup signals of future IBD.
Externally validated the model at a demographically distinct safety-net hospital and simulated a diagnosis-code-only alert workflow.
infographic.evidence_signal: At 6 months after presentation, Mamba achieved AUROC 0.969 at UCSF and 0.965 at ZSFG, with median lead times of 20 and 15 months, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: This was a retrospective study, so real-world alert performance, false positives, and impact on outcomes still need prospective evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Prediction of incident inflammatory bowel disease from routine electronic health records: development and external validation of a longitudinal machine learning model

title: Can GPT Be Used as an Alternative Prediction Model to Traditional Machine Learning and Neural Networks on Low-Volume Clinical Data?
authors: Bin Akter, S.; Akter, S.; Eisenberg, D.; Hill, C.; Lotvola, A.; Fresneda Fernandez, J.; Sarkar Pias, T.; Rafiqul Islam, M.; Islam, H.
abstract: Background and ObjectiveEarly and reliable disease prediction from structured clinical data remains challenging when datasets are small, highly imbalanced, and contain limited positive disease cases. Conventional machine learning (ML) and deep learning approaches often struggle to capture clinically meaningful relationships under such low-data representation conditions due to weak statistical associations between features and prediction targets. This study proposes a clinically grounded Distil GPT2-based table-to-text framework for disease prediction using structured healthcare datasets, motivated by the contextual reasoning capability of GPT models to better capture clinically meaningful relationships when statistical learning alone becomes insufficient due to limited data availability. Methods & MaterialsStructured clinical records were transformed into physician-style textual descriptions and enriched through GPT4-generated medical paraphrasing to improve minority-class representation while preserving clinical meaning. Both the original and generated clinical texts were used to fine-tune a Distil GPT2 model across four public healthcare datasets, including heart disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and thyroid cancer recurrence. Gradient-based explainable AI analysis was additionally incorporated to identify clinically important features influencing prediction outcomes. ResultsThe proposed framework demonstrated consistently strong predictive performance across four clinical datasets, achieving average precision, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.96, 0.97, 0.96, and 0.96, respectively. The model achieved improved sensitivity, stronger generalization, and more stable predictive behavior compared with traditional ML, deep learning, transformer-based, and GAN-augmented approaches. Importantly, the framework consistently emphasized clinically meaningful variables even under severe class imbalance, where conventional ML and neural network models often struggled to identify key clinically relevant relationships. ConclusionsThe proposed Distil GPT2-based table-to-text framework provides a practical and clinically interpretable approach for disease prediction from limited structured healthcare data. By integrating contextual clinical reasoning with explainable prediction mechanisms, the framework suggests strong potential for early risk detection, transparent clinical decision support, and reliable deployment in real-world data-scarce healthcare settings.

infographic.key_insight: A DistilGPT2 table-to-text approach can turn small, imbalanced clinical datasets into strong disease prediction models by leveraging contextual language patterns rather than relying only on traditional feature statistics.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help improve early disease risk prediction in low-volume clinical settings where conventional machine learning models often miss minority-case patterns.
method: Converted structured patient records into physician-style text descriptions
Augmented minority-class examples with GPT-4-generated medical paraphrases
Fine-tuned DistilGPT2 and used gradient-based explainability to highlight important clinical features
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four public datasets, the model reported average precision, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.96, 0.97, 0.96, and 0.96, respectively, with stronger sensitivity and stability than several comparison methods.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from public datasets, so real-world performance and safety need external validation before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Can GPT Be Used as an Alternative Prediction Model to Traditional Machine Learning and Neural Networks on Low-Volume Clinical Data?

title: MRI Biomarkers for Brain Metastases in Lung Cancer Using Machine Learning
authors: Chadha, S.; Sritharan, D. V.; Sharma, R.; Dolezal, D.; Chande, S.; Breuer, G.; Fu, D.; Gupta, A.; Hossain, J. O.; Srinivasan, A.; Weiss, D.; Chiang, V. L.; Nguyen, D. X.; Aneja, S.
abstract: PurposeExisting prognostic models for brain metastases from lung cancer rely on clinical variables and do not capture the biological heterogeneity of host or tumor factors underlying survival outcomes. We evaluated whether MRI-derived radiomic biomarkers improve prognostic stratification beyond clinical variables. We also investigated their biological correlates using matched histopathology. Experimental DesignThis retrospective study included 103 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer and matched pre-operative MRI and histopathology. Radiomic features from T1-weighted contrast-enhanced and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were combined with clinical variables to train Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and DeepSurv models for overall survival (OS), CNS progression, and leptomeningeal (LM) progression. Risk groups from an imaging-only model were compared for clinical and histopathologic differences. ResultsImaging features improved prognostic performance beyond clinical variables across all modeling frameworks, with the combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieving the highest concordance index for OS (0.728). Risk groups from the best-performing model for each endpoint differed significantly in OS (median 26.7 vs. 9.1 months, p < 0.001) and LM progression (p = 0.003), but not in CNS progression. Imaging-only risk groups did not differ significantly in any clinical variable, but high-risk patients were less likely to have tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (46% vs. 77%, p = 0.010) and PD-L1 expression [≥] 50% (10% vs. 32%, p = 0.049). ConclusionsMRI radiomic biomarkers provide prognostic information beyond established clinical variables in lung cancer brain metastases and correspond to features of the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting their potential to refine risk stratification. Statement of Translational RelevanceBrain metastases affect 30-40% of patients with lung cancer. Existing prognostic models rely on clinical variables, which do not fully capture the biological heterogeneity that drives outcomes. We show that machine learning models integrating MRI-derived radiomic features with clinical variables improve prognostic discrimination beyond clinical variables alone. Because these biomarkers are derived from standard-of-care pre-operative imaging, they can be generated without additional testing or delay to treatment planning. Using matched histopathology from resected lesions, we further show that imaging-defined risk groups do not simply reproduce established clinical risk factors but instead correspond to differences in the tumor immune microenvironment, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression. These findings support the use of quantitative imaging biomarkers as a non-invasive method to refine risk stratification at diagnosis, informing treatment selection and clinical trial enrollment for patients with brain metastases from lung cancer.

infographic.key_insight: MRI radiomic features from pre-operative brain scans added prognostic value beyond clinical variables for lung cancer brain metastases, and the imaging risk groups appeared to reflect underlying immune-tumor biology.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If validated, this approach could help identify patients at higher risk of death or leptomeningeal progression and support more personalized follow-up and treatment planning.
method: Retrospective cohort of 103 lung cancer patients with brain metastases and matched MRI/histopathology.
Extracted radiomic features from contrast-enhanced T1 and FLAIR MRI sequences.
Compared Cox models, random survival forests, and DeepSurv using clinical, imaging, and combined inputs for OS, CNS progression, and LM progression.
infographic.evidence_signal: The combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieved the best overall survival concordance index (0.728), and imaging-only risk groups showed differences in tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center retrospective data with a modest sample size means the findings need external validation before routine clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: MRI Biomarkers for Brain Metastases in Lung Cancer Using Machine Learning

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease
authors: Caiola, M.; Thompson, T.; Stephens, S. B.; Salamat, B.; Harris, K.; Lara, C.; Coban-Akdemir, Z.; Zhang, L.; Roth, M.; Milosavljevic, A.; Weitz, A. C.; Morris, S. A.
abstract: BackgroundGenetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. MethodsRetrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class-balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. ResultsThe cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). ConclusionsRoutine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

infographic.key_insight: Routine clinical data available at the first echocardiogram can help shortlist the most likely genetic conditions in infants with congenital heart disease.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could support earlier genetic suspicion and triage in CHD care, especially before definitive genetic testing results are available.
method: Retrospective single-center cohort of 1,720 children with congenital heart disease and known genetic testing status.
Compared class-balanced logistic regression with a multimodal deep learning fusion model as more data became available over time.
Evaluated balanced top-3 accuracy after echocardiogram data, then after serial records, radiology notes, and ICD-10 codes were added.
infographic.evidence_signal: Balanced top-3 accuracy was 0.758 using echocardiogram-visit data alone and increased to 0.809 with later clinical codes; multimodal fusion performed similarly.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center retrospective data and moderate class imbalance may limit generalizability, and the model should be validated prospectively before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease

title: FERMAT: An Autoregressive Clinical Foundation Model for Disease Risk and Clinical Event Prediction
authors: Jung, J.; Lee, H.-C.
abstract: Clinical foundation models learn patterns in longitudinal health records that can be reused across prediction tasks. However, the relative strengths of representation-based and generation-based prediction across clinical tasks remain unclear. Using longitudinal electronic health records from 3.77 million patients at a single hospital, we developed FERMAT (Foundation model for Exploring Real-world Multimodal health data using Autoregressive Trajectory modeling), a 65-million-parameter clinical foundation model. We compared predictions from task-specific predictors trained on patient representations with those derived from generated clinical event sequences. Representation-based prediction performed better in the disease-risk comparisons. In detailed analyses of five-year chronic kidney disease, fatty liver, and diabetes risk in a test cohort of 10,000 patients, representation-based predictors exceeded generation-based estimates by 0.098-0.115 in observation-weighted AUROC and had lower probability error. Generation-based prediction, in turn, performed better in predicting diagnoses, prescriptions, and procedures recorded on the same day, a task motivated by the frequent presence of multiple events with the same date in hospital EHRs. Using 50 generated trajectories per patient, it achieved a Recall@10 of 71.0%, compared with 55.7% for representation-based prediction, with a paired improvement of 15.31 percentage points (95% CI, 13.92-16.79; n = 1,862). These findings demonstrate task-dependent strengths of representation-based and generation-based applications within a single clinical foundation model, providing an empirical basis for exploring how the two approaches can be used individually or combined to address clinical prediction needs.

infographic.key_insight: FERMAT shows that the best prediction approach depends on the task: representation-based methods work better for future disease risk, while generation-based methods are stronger for same-day clinical event prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests clinical foundation models may need to combine both prediction styles to better support risk stratification and near-term event forecasting in real-world EHR settings.
method: Trained a 65M-parameter autoregressive clinical foundation model on longitudinal EHRs from 3.77 million patients.
Compared representation-based predictors with generation-based forecasts across disease risk and clinical event tasks.
Evaluated performance on chronic kidney disease, fatty liver, diabetes, and same-day diagnoses, prescriptions, and procedures.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a 10,000-patient test cohort, representation-based prediction improved five-year disease-risk AUROC by 0.098-0.115, while generation-based prediction reached 71.0% Recall@10 for same-day events versus 55.7% for representation-based methods.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a single-hospital EHR dataset, so performance may not generalize across health systems or documentation practices.
infographic.paper_title: FERMAT: An Autoregressive Clinical Foundation Model for Disease Risk and Clinical Event Prediction

title: RadKev: An Open-Weight Decision Model for Radiology
authors: Ram, U.; Zhang, R.
abstract: BackgroundMany radiology decisions, such as whether a report describes a finding or how urgently a study should be read, are choices among a fixed set of answers. Decision models return a probability for each permitted answer in one step, without generating text, and an open-weight model can run within a hospital so that patient data stay local. No decision model has yet been specialized for radiology and compared with large language models (LLMs). MethodsWe fine-tuned the general-purpose decision models Kev-27B (Qwen3.8-27B backbone) and Kev-9B on 36,109 records from public radiology datasets to obtain RadKev-27B and RadKev-9B, and compared them with the Kev models, the hosted decision models Jev and OpenAI Decisions, and the LLM Qwen3.8-27B, on 14,142 held-out questions in fifteen tasks (report reading, case diagnosis and classification, radiological knowledge). The prespecified primary outcome was task-averaged accuracy relative to Kev-27B. ResultsRadKev-27B exceeded Kev-27B by 4.9 percentage points (95% CI 3.8 to 6.2), with the largest gain in report error detection (22.6 points); RadKev-9B exceeded Kev-9B by 6.9 points (5.5 to 8.4) and did not differ detectably from Kev-27B, a model three times its size. RadKev-27B was more accurate than the hosted decision models Jev (3.0 points, 1.7 to 4.4) and OpenAI Decisions (4.8, 3.2 to 6.4), than Qwen3.8-27B without reasoning (4.7, 3.4 to 6.0) and with reasoning (2.8 points, 1.0 to 4.6) on 1,675 questions, at 132-fold lower latency (128 ms vs 16.9 s per question). At an error rate of 5%, RadKev-27B could answer 90.5% of questions and Kev-27B 76.4%. ConclusionsRadKev-27B was more accurate than two hosted decision models and an LLM of the same size, with or without reasoning, at a fraction of the latency of reasoning, and can be deployed within an institution for categorical radiology decisions after validation on local data.

infographic.key_insight: RadKev is an open-weight decision model specialized for radiology that improves categorical radiology decisions over its general-purpose base model and matched or exceeded larger or hosted alternatives.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Because it can run inside a hospital and keep data local, RadKev could support faster, privacy-preserving radiology triage and decision support after local validation.
method: Fine-tuned Kev-27B and Kev-9B on 36,109 public radiology records to create RadKev-27B and RadKev-9B.
Compared against base Kev models, hosted decision models, and Qwen3.8-27B on 14,142 held-out questions across 15 radiology tasks.
Evaluated accuracy and latency, with task-averaged accuracy as the prespecified primary outcome.
infographic.evidence_signal: RadKev-27B improved over Kev-27B by 4.9 percentage points and was more accurate than Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Qwen3.8-27B, while running about 132 times faster than reasoning mode on a 1,675-question comparison set.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was shown on held-out public datasets, so real-world deployment still needs validation on local workflows, scanner populations, and reporting practices.
infographic.paper_title: RadKev: An Open-Weight Decision Model for Radiology

title: Introducing Infrastructure as Code for deployment and governance of medical AI: A case study
authors: Vogel, M.; Reuter, N.; Ruf, S.; Noori, A.; Madrid, J.; Balicer, R.; Witzenrath, M.; Sander, L. E.; Groeschel, M. I.
abstract: Clinical AI deployment rarely reaches the bedside because both workstation integration and governed backend provisioning are challenging. We introduce a workflow that allows rapid and governed access to AI functionalities through a browser interface or API, enabling privacy-compliant data analysis. The complex setup for compliant healthcare applications such as a secure backend, private AI model endpoint, and managed identity configuration is encoded by itself, a concept known as Infrastructure as Code (IaC). IaC is a concept in which networks, access rights, and service endpoints are written down as machine-readable files that can be reviewed once and executed identically in any institution. Here, we apply this concept to a clinical use case. The process of deploying a governed, private clinical AI solution using this approach in a tertiary care center took, on average, 310.3 {+/-} 196.6 seconds (n=25, mean {+/-} SD). To further demonstrate the clinical value of this approach, we developed and deployed an LLM-based inconsistency checker, which identifies textual inconsistency in medical documents. When evaluating the tool on a set of 1,347 physician-approved clinical documents, the tool flagged a clinically severe inconsistency in 105 clinical documents (7.8%, approximately 1 in 13). In a severity-stratified physician audit, 149 of 150 sampled findings were confirmed (population-weighted PPV 98.2%; CI 94.8 - 100.0). In summary, we present the application of IaC frameworks to a healthcare use case and demonstrate that clinically useful AI applications can be deployed to physician workstations in hospital-governed cloud environments within a few minutes. DescriptionTo overcome the implementation barriers for use of AI in healthcare, we adapted Infrastructure as Code to a clinical use case and deployed a hospital-governed large language model service that clinicians reach from a browser without workstation software. Provisioned by Infrastructure as Code the service became available in 310 seconds on average, and its first clinical application, an inconsistency checker, detected inconsistencies in clinical documents with high positive predictive value.

infographic.key_insight: Infrastructure as Code can rapidly deploy governed, hospital-controlled AI services for clinical use through a browser or API.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may make it easier for hospitals to deliver privacy-compliant AI tools to clinicians without installing workstation software.
method: Encoded secure backend, private AI endpoint, and identity/access setup as machine-readable infrastructure files.
Deployed a hospital-governed LLM service accessible from a browser or API.
Built an inconsistency checker to flag contradictory statements in clinical documents.
infographic.evidence_signal: Deployment took 310.3 ± 196.6 seconds on average (n=25), and the inconsistency checker flagged severe inconsistencies in 105 of 1,347 physician-approved documents; 149 of 150 sampled findings were confirmed (population-weighted PPV 98.2%).
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a single tertiary-care case study, so broader generalizability and integration burden may vary across institutions.
infographic.paper_title: Introducing Infrastructure as Code for deployment and governance of medical AI: A case study

title: Cross-database adaptation of machine learning models for predicting sustained antibiotic exposure among patients with intracerebral hemorrhage in intensive care units
authors: Pathak, S.; Si, Y.; Sanjaya, J.; Haghi, M.; Kudrot, N. T.; Placencia, G.; Alaei, K.; Pishgar, M.
abstract: BackgroundPatients with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in intensive care units (ICUs) frequently receive antibiotics early in critical illness. Such exposure reflects suspected infection, physiological deterioration, monitoring intensity, and clinical management and may vary across institutions and electronic health record databases. We evaluated target-domain adaptation for modeling sustained antibiotic exposure in critically ill patients with ICH. MethodsWe analyzed derived ICH cohorts from MIMIC-IV and the eICU Collaborative Research Database. MIMIC-IV included 2,024 ICU stays and served as the source cohort. The eICU cohort comprised 1,277 stays and was divided, at the ICU-stay level, into a development subset (766 stays) and a held-out evaluation subset (511 stays). The eICU outcome was sustained antibiotic exposure on at least two ICU days. Candidate models incorporated demographic, comorbidity, physiological, laboratory, neurologic, respiratory, temporal, and measurementprocess features. Timestamped observations for static and temporal tabular families were censored at the recorded first-antibiotic time when available, whereas the compact sequence component and explicit measurement-density features used the full first 24 hours. For base-model families using eICU development data, meta-learner inputs were generated by five-fold stratified cross-fitting. A 42-input L2-penalized logistic meta-learner combined 16 model probabilities with model-summary, clinical, availability, and measurement-density features. ResultsThe held-out eICU subset contained 48 positive outcomes (9.39%). The adapted ensemble achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.841 (95% CI 0.775-0.899) and an average precision (AP) of 0.540 (95% CI 0.399-0.676), with a Brier score of 0.063 and expected calibration error of 0.029. The MIMIC-IV source-only stack achieved an AUROC of 0.782; the paired AUROC difference was 0.059 (95% CI 0.003-0.112). In a separate patient-grouped five-fold out-of-fold sensitivity analysis of 503 linked eICU stays, AUROC was 0.807 (95% CI 0.691-0.910). ConclusionsTarget-domain adaptation improved held-out discrimination relative to a source-only stack for sustained antibiotic exposure. Because some model components and measurement-process features used information from the broader first 24 hours, the model should be interpreted as a first-24-hour treatment-association model rather than a strictly prospective pre-treatment infection predictor.

infographic.key_insight: An adapted machine-learning ensemble better predicted sustained antibiotic exposure in ICU patients with intracerebral hemorrhage across hospitals than a source-only model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests prediction models for antibiotic use in critical care may need site-specific adaptation before being trusted for decision support or benchmarking.
method: Derived ICH ICU cohorts from MIMIC-IV (source) and eICU (target).
Built multiple feature-based base models using demographic, comorbidity, physiologic, lab, neurologic, respiratory, temporal, and measurement-density data.
Combined model outputs with clinical and data-availability features in a 42-input L2-penalized logistic meta-learner using cross-fitting.
infographic.evidence_signal: On held-out eICU data (511 stays, 48 positives), the adapted ensemble reached AUROC 0.841 and AP 0.540, outperforming the MIMIC-IV source-only stack (AUROC 0.782).
infographic.watch_item: Performance was evaluated retrospectively and the target outcome is proxy-based and institution-dependent, so external transportability and real-world implementation still need confirmation.
infographic.paper_title: Cross-database adaptation of machine learning models for predicting sustained antibiotic exposure among patients with intracerebral hemorrhage in intensive care units

title: AI-assisted identification of potential treatment injury from inpatient discharge summaries: an early-stage sociotechnical evaluation in a New Zealand district hospital
authors: Bhatnagar, P.; Fearnley, W.
abstract: ObjectivesTo assess the feasibility and early performance of an AI-assisted workflow screening inpatient discharge summaries for potential treatment injury requiring clinician review and possible Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) consideration in New Zealand. DesignSingle-site, six-month quality-improvement/service-evaluation pilot using a large language model as an index screening tool with clinician adjudication. SettingWairarapa Hospital, New Zealand. ParticipantsAll inpatient discharge summaries produced during the pilot period (n=2,642). InterventionsThe model generated structured candidate harm signals with supporting text and certainty labels. Clinicians reviewed all flagged cases and determined whether escalation was appropriate. Main outcome measuresScreening yield, positive predictive value (PPV) for clinician-adjudicated iatrogenic harm, unsupported outputs, overlap with incident reporting and ACC claims, and clinician workload. ResultsThe workflow generated 237 candidate signals (yield 9.0%, 95% CI 7.9% to 10.1%). Clinicians classified 102 as confirmed iatrogenic harm, 43 as possible harm, 81 as no harm and 11 as unsupported outputs. PPV was 43.0% for confirmed harm (95% CI 36.8% to 49.4%) and 61.2% for confirmed-or-possible harm (95% CI 54.9% to 67.1%); unsupported outputs occurred in 4.6%. Seven ACC claims were lodged following AI-assisted identification. Of 68 organisational ACC claims during the same period, 17 overlapped with AI-identified cases. The workflow required approximately 25-30 minutes of clinician time per week. ConclusionsAI-assisted discharge-summary screening was operationally feasible and increased visibility of potential treatment injuries for clinician review. Further prospective evaluation should use an independent chart-review reference standard to estimate diagnostic accuracy and assess equity, workload and implementation outcomes. RegistrationNot applicable. Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSHealthcare-associated harm is systematically under-detected, with incident reporting and administrative data capturing only a fraction of treatment injuries. Structured record review methods such as the Global Trigger Tool identify substantially higher rates of adverse events but are resource-intensive and difficult to sustain at scale. What this study addsThis study demonstrates that an AI-assisted workflow can feasibly screen inpatient discharge summaries to identify potential treatment injuries for clinician review within routine workflows. The findings suggest that AI can function as a form of visibility infrastructure, surfacing harm signals not consistently captured by existing reporting systems while preserving clinician judgement and governance processes. How this study might affect research, practice or policyAI-assisted screening could strengthen patient safety surveillance and support more consistent consideration of treatment injury within compensation systems. Future research should evaluate diagnostic accuracy, equity impacts, and workflow design, including whether carefully governed automation of administrative steps can improve escalation processes without displacing clinical oversight. DisclaimerThe AI system generated candidate signals of potential treatment injury only. Final determination of treatment injury status and ACC eligibility remained the responsibility of clinicians and the Accident Compensation Corporation through standard statutory processes.

infographic.key_insight: A large-language-model screening workflow can feasibly flag potential treatment injuries from discharge summaries for clinician review, but many signals still need adjudication.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may help hospitals surface previously missed inpatient harms for possible ACC consideration, supporting safer follow-up and reporting workflows.
method: Single-site, six-month pilot at Wairarapa Hospital using all 2,642 inpatient discharge summaries.
LLM generated structured harm signals with supporting text and certainty labels.
Clinicians reviewed flagged cases and decided whether escalation was warranted.
infographic.evidence_signal: The system flagged 237 cases (9.0% yield); clinicians confirmed 102 as iatrogenic harm and judged 43 more as possible harm, with 4.6% unsupported outputs.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from one hospital and clinician review without an independent chart-review gold standard, so accuracy and equity effects remain uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: AI-assisted identification of potential treatment injury from inpatient discharge summaries: an early-stage sociotechnical evaluation in a New Zealand district hospital

title: Automated Variant Prioritization in Suspected Genetic Kidney Disease
authors: Rank, N.; Lukassen, S.; Anderegg, M.; Eckardt, K.-U.; Halbritter, J. P.; Popp, B.
abstract: IntroductionDespite the identification of >700 genes associated with inherited kidney disease, many affected individuals presumably remain genetically undiagnosed through testing of known disease genes. Novel disease gene discovery requires interpretation of large-scale sequencing data, which remains challenging. MethodsWe developed the Nephro Candidate Score (N-CS), a machine learning (ML) framework for variant prioritization combining a Nephro Gene Score (N-GS), Nephro Variant Score (N-VS), and heuristic Inheritance Score. The ML-based N-GS and N-VS predict gene-disease relevance and variant pathogenicity from diverse genomic features. Clinical utility was assessed in 1452 individuals with suspected inherited kidney disease using exome-wide candidate discovery and gene-level burden analysis, with external validation using recently proposed inherited kidney disease genes. ResultsThe N-CS showed strong predictive performance, with the XGBoost-based N-GS achieving an AUC of 0.94 and the Logistic Regression-based N-VS an AUC of 0.99 on independent test sets. A gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated significant enrichment of kidney-related biological processes among top-ranked genes (p < 0.001). In our patient cohort, N-CS-guided variant filtering recovered established disease genes and highlighted ERMP1 as a compelling candidate. Incorporating the N-GS in a polycystic kidney disease burden analysis reduced multiple-testing penalties, highlighting a moderate-effect candidate. Externally, the N-CS assigned high scores to 10 of 11 newly proposed kidney disease genes. ConclusionThe N-CS is a digital framework to accelerate disease gene discovery and diagnosis. It is freely available as the NC-Scorer web tool (https://nc-scorer.kidney-genetics.org/) and a command-line interface enabling standardized, scalable candidate variant evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: The Nephro Candidate Score (N-CS) uses machine learning to rank genes and variants that may explain suspected inherited kidney disease, helping surface plausible disease candidates from large sequencing datasets.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This tool could speed up interpretation of exome data in patients with suspected genetic kidney disease and support more standardized candidate variant prioritization in research and diagnostic workflows.
method: Combines a Nephro Gene Score, Nephro Variant Score, and an inheritance-based heuristic into one prioritization framework.
Uses XGBoost to estimate gene-disease relevance and logistic regression to estimate variant pathogenicity from genomic features.
Evaluated with exome-wide candidate discovery, gene-level burden analysis, and external validation against newly proposed kidney disease genes.
infographic.evidence_signal: In independent test sets, the N-GS achieved AUC 0.94 and the N-VS achieved AUC 0.99, with enrichment of kidney-related pathways among top-ranked genes and high scores for 10 of 11 external candidate genes.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was shown in retrospective and validation datasets, so prospective clinical impact and generalizability across diverse populations and sequencing pipelines still need confirmation.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Variant Prioritization in Suspected Genetic Kidney Disease

title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Clinical and Genomic Prognostic Factors for Progression-Free Survival in Metastatic Breast Cancer Using Phase III MONALEESA Trials
authors: Wang, C.; Paul, R.; Li, Y.; Smith, S.; Cao, Q.; Chang, S. H.; Charlab, R.; Coroller, T.; Huang, R.; Amiri-Kordestani, L.; Li, Z.; Liu, Q.; Osgood, C.; Peyrard, S.; Sahiner, B.; Santana-Quintero, L.; Su, F.; Zarate, J. P.; Zhu, H.; Ohlssen, D.; Petrick, N.; Amatya, A.; Solovieff, N.
abstract: PurposeCyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors in combination with endocrine therapy have become widely adopted as a first-line treatment approach for hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2-) advanced breast cancer (ABC). Through a collaboration between Novartis and the US Food and Drug Administration, we integrated multimodal data from phase III MONALEESA trials to identify novel prognostic factors for HR+/HER2-ABC. Experimental DesignBaseline clinical and genomics data were collected from patients in the MONALEESA-2, -3, and -7 trials. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from plasma samples and gene expression in archival tumor biopsies were analyzed. Machine learning models were trained (n = 1,355) on progression-free survival (PFS) using multimodal features via fusion models. In a test set (n = 382), prognostic performances were evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier, Cox, and Weibull models. ResultsThe late fusion model achieved a prognostic performance (C-index: 0.727, 95% CI: 0.641-0.799) slightly outperforming early fusion (C-index: 0.718, 95% CI: 0.631-0.791) and single-modality models. Model-based risk stratification identified distinct low- and high-risk groups (PFS HR, 0.28; 95% CI: 0.20-0.38). Among the top 40 features for progression risk (18 clinical, 20 gene expression, and 2 ctDNA), these were associated with higher risk: liver involvement, higher histological grades, early relapse; lower STC2 and RBBP8 expressions and higher FBX05 expression; and higher tumor mutational burden and ctDNA purity. ConclusionsIntegrating clinical and genomic modalities improved progression risk prediction compared with single-modality models, while highlighting salient features that inform the underlying biology and support hypothesis generation.

infographic.key_insight: Combining clinical, tumor genomics, and ctDNA data with machine learning modestly improved progression-free survival risk prediction for HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This multimodal approach may help better identify patients at higher or lower risk of progression, supporting more informed prognostic assessment in advanced breast cancer.
method: Trained fusion-based machine learning models on baseline clinical, ctDNA, and gene expression data from MONALEESA-2, -3, and -7.
Compared early fusion, late fusion, and single-modality models for progression-free survival prediction.
Evaluated performance in a held-out test set using Kaplan-Meier, Cox, and Weibull analyses.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the test set (n=382), the late fusion model achieved C-index 0.727, slightly better than early fusion (0.718) and single-modality approaches, with clear low- vs high-risk separation.
infographic.watch_item: The gains over simpler models were modest, so external validation and real-world testing are needed before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Clinical and Genomic Prognostic Factors for Progression-Free Survival in Metastatic Breast Cancer Using Phase III MONALEESA Trials

title: Provider Experiences with AI Clinical Decision Support in eSanjeevani
authors: Bhagat, P.; Rana, S.; Kaur, K. N.; Sivasubramanian, S.; Garg, V.; Khalikar, S.; Dutta, T.; Chander, A.; Sood, S.; Singh, H.
abstract: BackgroundClinical decision support systems (CDSS) are increasingly embedded in national telemedicine services, however how different stakeholders who use them experience these tools, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, is less explored. In the assisted model of Indias eSanjeevani service, spoke health workers enter structured symptoms and hub clinicians review a symptom summary and an artificial intelligence (AI)-generated differential diagnosis. ObjectiveTo describe role-specific experiences of eSanjeevanis CDSS functions and to estimate how acceptance coexists with specific reported difficulties within each role. MethodsWe analyzed a program feedback web survey completed between 11 July and 29 July, 2025 by hub clinicians and spoke providers. Prespecified item profiles covered review of summaries and suggested diagnoses, the perceived relation of suggestions to the clinicians own diagnosis, ease of use and intention to use (hub), and symptom-capture utility, question quantity, question relevance, summary presentation and satisfaction (spoke). Within-role contrasts were reported as absolute differences in acceptance with Newcombe 95% CIs. Short open comments underwent content analysis. ResultsThe cohort comprised 190 hub and 662 spoke respondents from 13 and 15 states (21.4% and 19.3% of eligible providers). Among hub respondents, 76.8% regularly reviewed the symptom summary and 58.9% the suggested diagnoses; 72.6% judged suggestions matched (32.6%) or appropriate but different (40.0%), 7.9% mostly inappropriate, and 11.1% reported that suggestions were mostly not generated. Overall, 85.3% intended to keep using the tools. Affirmative intention was 98.4% when suggestions matched, 66.7% when they were mostly inappropriate (difference vs matched or appropriate-23.2 percentage points, 95% CI-48.5 to-4.0) and 61.9% when mostly absent (-25.7, 95% CI-47.1 to-7.3); technical issues, reported by 38.4%, made little difference (-2.8, 95% CI-14.1 to 7.3). Among spoke respondents, 63.4% rated question quantity appropriate, with miscalibration in both directions (15.6% too many; 16.6% too few); 89.9% found the questions relevant and 91.8% found the summary clear. Satisfaction was 75.3% and did not differ materially between those reporting too many questions and those reporting an appropriate number (-2.7, 95% CI-12.8 to 6.0). Comments located spoke difficulties in question burden and missing complaints, and hub difficulties in freezing and in the scope and availability of suggestions. Estimates were stable across cohort, ambiguity and state-exclusion sensitivity analyses. ConclusionsAcceptance of eSanjeevanis CDSS was high in both roles. For hub clinicians it tracked the perceived quality and availability of AI suggestions rather than technical friction; spoke workers accepted the question burden, but its two-directional miscalibration points toward complaint-specific, adaptive questioning. These provider reports do not measure diagnostic accuracy. They identify log-based and audit-based indicators that the next evaluation cycle should measure directly.

infographic.key_insight: In India’s eSanjeevani telemedicine service, both hub clinicians and spoke providers generally accepted AI clinical decision support, but acceptance varied when the AI output felt inaccurate, incomplete, or poorly calibrated to the case.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI decision support was viewed as useful for triage and review workflows, but its real-world value depends on reliable symptom capture, relevant questions, and actionable diagnostic suggestions.
method: Program feedback web survey of hub clinicians and spoke providers in eSanjeevani
Compared acceptance and difficulty patterns within each role using absolute differences with Newcombe 95% CIs
Included short open-ended comments analyzed for recurring themes
infographic.evidence_signal: Survey data from 190 hub and 662 spoke respondents across 13 and 15 Indian states showed high intention to continue use, with lower acceptance when suggestions were mostly inappropriate or absent.
infographic.watch_item: The findings come from a short voluntary feedback survey, so results may reflect response bias and may not capture longer-term workflow effects or patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Provider Experiences with AI Clinical Decision Support in eSanjeevani

title: IVA, a locally deployable Intelligent Variant Analyser based on a small language model for complete case-level and trio-based genomic interpretation.
authors: Santoni, F.; Ducret, E.; Oreshkov, S.; Abdur, R.; Frederiksen, H.; Ullah, M.; laverre, a.; forey, r.; Le caignec, c.; Ansar, M.
abstract: BackgroundRecent work has brought large language models (LLMs) into clinical variant interpretation. In most existing approaches, the model is confined to text-level operations, retrieving, extracting, compacting, and summarizing heterogeneous evidence, while the genuine genetic evaluation is delegated to a separate deterministic engine. Other tools employ LLMs to mine functional evidence for a single ACMG criterion, to rerank a classifiers output, or to answer isolated variant questions. Integrative genetic reasoning, by contrast, demands multi-source evidence weighing for each variant, reconciliation of inheritance with observed zygosity and parental genotypes, joint interpretation of variants in the same gene, and the derivation of a case-level conclusion. Moreover, to protect patient privacy, this must be done on hospital premises. Methodso build an end-to-end variant interpreter that runs on local infrastructure, we benchmarked 13 small language models (SLMs) on 150 multiple-choice genetics questions and selected Qwen3.5-9B. In IVA (Intelligent Variant Analyser), a four-stage pipeline, the model assigns ACMG/AMP criteria, applies de novo, dominant, recessive, and X-linked inheritance logic to trios, and writes a structured report, while deterministic code handles retrieval, phasing, point summation, citation checking, and formatting. We evaluated IVA on synthetic scenarios, 16 solved trios, and 327 solved singleton cases of visual impairment, on a single GPU. ResultsOn the benchmark, Qwen3.5-9B reached a mean accuracy of 0.81, compared with 0.89 for a 1.6-trillion-parameter cloud model. In the 16 trios, IVA reported every previously identified pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or uncertain-significance variant of interest (sensitivity 100%; precision 39.5%). In the 327 singleton cases, it recovered 93% of the expert-reported causative variants and classified 82% of them as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (precision 43%). Failures fell into four recurrent classes: omission, unverified mechanism, mismatch between reasoning and label, and arithmetic errors. ConclusionsA small language model running on local hardware can serve as the reasoning layer for case-level and trio-based variant interpretation when it is surrounded by deterministic safeguards. Because its outputs are not deterministic, analyst review and prospective multicenter validation remain necessary. DescriptionIVA is a locally deployable pipeline in which a sub-10B small language model assigns ACMG/AMP criteria, reasons over free text phenotype descriptions, familial inheritance, and writes the clinical report for a complete candidate-variant table, with all model inference running on hospital hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A locally deployable small language model can perform case-level and trio-based genomic interpretation by combining ACMG/AMP evidence assignment with inheritance reasoning and deterministic checks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could enable privacy-preserving variant interpretation on hospital infrastructure, supporting more complete genomic reporting without relying on cloud-based models.
method: Benchmarked 13 small language models on 150 genetics multiple-choice questions and selected Qwen3.5-9B.
Built a four-stage IVA pipeline that assigns ACMG/AMP criteria, applies inheritance logic, and generates structured reports.
Used deterministic code for retrieval, phasing, scoring, citation checking, and formatting.
infographic.evidence_signal: IVA was evaluated on synthetic scenarios, 16 solved trios, and 327 solved singleton visual impairment cases, recovering 100% of trio variants of interest and 93% of causative singleton variants.
infographic.watch_item: Precision was modest and failures included omission, unverified mechanism claims, reasoning-to-label mismatches, and arithmetic errors, so human review remains essential.
infographic.paper_title: IVA, a locally deployable Intelligent Variant Analyser based on a small language model for complete case-level and trio-based genomic interpretation.

title: COVID-19 vaccination and survival of cancer patients in Northwestern Russia: a historical registry-based cohort study
authors: Dyachenko, A. A.; Bogdanov, M. A.; Bogdanov, D. V.; Meldo, A. A.; Chernina, V. Y.; Gombolevskiy, V. A.; Grjibovski, A. M.; Valkov, M. Y.
abstract: BackgroundCancer patients face a significantly elevated risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes. Although vaccination is a cornerstone of prevention, data on vaccination coverage and association with survival among Russian cancer patients remain scarce. We assessed COVID-19 vaccination coverage and its association with overall survival in a population-based cohort of cancer patients in Northwest Russia. MethodsThis retrospective registry-based cohort study integrated data from the Population-Based Cancer Registry (PBCR) of the Arkhangelsk Region and the Nenets Autonomous Okrug, regional vaccination records, and an artificial intelligence (AI)-based analysis of chest computed tomography (CT) scans. The cohort consisted of 1,144 cancer patients who underwent CT between August 2020 and April 2021. Vaccination status was ascertained via data linkage. Overall survival (OS) was compared between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, adjusted for demographic, clinical, and AI-derived CT biomarkers. To mitigate immortal time bias, the primary analysis used a landmark approach restricted to patients alive on March 1, 2021 (N = 1,136). A sensitivity analysis used a November 1, 2021 landmark (N = 894). Vaccination status was defined as receipt of at least one dose before the landmark date. ResultsOnly 6.6% (n=76) of patients received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine (Sputnik V or Sputnik Light). Vaccinated patients were more likely to have earlier-stage cancer and were less likely to be receiving active treatment. In the primary landmark analysis, vaccination was associated with a significantly higher 3-year OS (80.3% vs. 45.7%, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, vaccination was independently associated with a 60% lower hazard of all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.25-0.64). AI-detected COVID-19 pneumonia on baseline CT was also an independent predictor of poorer survival (adjusted HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.09-1.59). In the sensitivity analysis (November 1, 2021 landmark), the adjusted HR for vaccination was 0.56 (95% CI 0.34-0.92), showing a consistent but attenuated association. ConclusionThis study reveals critically low COVID-19 vaccination coverage among cancer patients in Northwest Russia. Nevertheless, vaccination was strongly associated with a substantial survival benefit, underscoring its importance as a potentially lifesaving intervention for this vulnerable population.

infographic.key_insight: In this Russian cancer cohort, receiving at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose before the landmark date was associated with markedly better overall survival.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The finding supports vaccination as an important prevention strategy for cancer patients, while highlighting the value of CT-based risk markers for prognosis.
method: Population-based retrospective cohort of 1,144 cancer patients from regional registries in Northwest Russia
Vaccination status was linked from records and survival was analyzed with Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox models
AI-derived chest CT biomarkers and a landmark design were used to reduce immortal time bias
infographic.evidence_signal: Only 6.6% of patients were vaccinated; in the primary landmark analysis, vaccination was associated with 3-year OS of 80.3% vs 45.7% and an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.40.
infographic.watch_item: Observational registry data can show association but not prove causation, and the very low vaccination rate plus baseline differences between groups may limit generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: COVID-19 vaccination and survival of cancer patients in Northwestern Russia: a historical registry-based cohort study

title: Machine Learning-based Prediction of Pacing-Induced Cardiomyopathy in Patients with Atrioventricular Block Underlying Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction
authors: Lee, J.-W.; Do, U.; Kim, H. M.; Choi, M. J.; Shin, S. Y.; Park, S.; Kang, K.-W.
abstract: BackgroundPacing-induced cardiomyopathy (PICM) is a major complication of chronic right ventricular pacing and develops in up to 25% of patients. Reliable prediction of PICM may facilitate individualized pacing strategy selection; however, currently available approaches demonstrate limited discriminative performance. This study aimed to develop and validate machine learning (ML) models for predicting PICM in patients with atrioventricular block (AVB) underlying heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction. MethodsIn this multicenter prospective study derived from the RISK-PICM registry (January 2002 to January 2026), 125 patients with AVB who underwent pacemaker implantation were analyzed. PICM was defined as a [≥]10% reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) resulting in an LVEF <50%. Four ML algorithms, including logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost, were trained using stratified 4-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter optimization and model discrimination was evaluated. ResultsPICM developed in 41 patients (32.8%) during a median follow-up of 4.8 years. Male sex, pre-implant minimum QTc interval, and post-implant maximum QRS duration were significantly associated with PICM in univariable Cox regression. XGBoost achieved the highest discriminative performance (AUROC 0.831; sensitivity 0.805; specificity 0.845). Feature importance analysis identified baseline LVEF and post-implant maximum QRS duration as the most influential features. Model-derived risk stratification significantly differentiated high-risk and low-risk groups on Kaplan-Meier analysis (P < 0.001). ConclusionsML-based models, particularly XGBoost, demonstrated clinically meaningful performance for PICM and may support individualized pacing strategy selection in patients with AVB and underlying heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is NewC_ST_ABSO_LIIn pacing-dependent AVB patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF, ensemble ML (XGBoost) predicted PICM with an AUROC of 0.831. C_LIO_LIModel-derived risk stratification separated PICM-free survival (log-rank P<0.001). C_LI What Are the Clinical ImplicationsO_LIAn ML model combining baseline LVEF, paced QRS duration, and the full parameter set may guide individualized choice between right ventricular and conduction system pacing in AVB patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF. C_LIO_LIUsing paced QRS duration combined with baseline LVEF during temporary pacing in AVB patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF, this risk estimate could inform pacing-strategy selection before permanent implantation, enabling pre-emptive use of conduction system pacing in high-risk patients. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: An XGBoost model using clinical and ECG features predicted pacing-induced cardiomyopathy (PICM) in AV block patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction with good discrimination.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help identify higher-risk patients before or after pacemaker implantation, potentially informing pacing strategy and follow-up intensity.
method: Multicenter prospective RISK-PICM registry analysis of 125 AV block patients with pacemakers
Compared four machine learning models: logistic regression, SVM, random forest, and XGBoost
Used stratified 4-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter tuning to predict PICM
infographic.evidence_signal: PICM occurred in 41 of 125 patients (32.8%) over a median 4.8 years, and XGBoost had the best performance with AUROC 0.831, sensitivity 0.805, and specificity 0.845.
infographic.watch_item: The sample was modest and the model needs external validation and workflow testing before routine clinical use.
